title: Cap. 7 Quartum: sufficienter / efficaciter—death for elect by absolute saving will
latin: Quartum argumentum nobis praebebit receptissima illa inter omnes Theologos distinctio, qua dici solet, Christum pro omnibus mortuum fuisse sufficienter, pro electis mortuum efficaciter. Nam sicuti ex priore membro refutavimus illorum sententiam, qui negant Christi mortem ex decreto Dei esse omnibus hominibus remedium applicabile, ita ex hoc posteriore illi sunt refutandi, qui negant Christi mortem, idque ex decreto Dei, esse remedium electis efficaciter & infallibiliter applicandum. Quis enim potest esse alius sensus horum verborum, Mortuus est pro electis efficaciter, quam, Mortuus est absoluta intentione & efficaci voluntate servandi electos?
pass_a_gloss: A fourth argument will furnish us that most received distinction among all Theologians, by which it is customarily said that Christ died for all sufficiently, for the elect efficaciously. For just as from the former member we refuted the opinion of those who deny that the death of Christ by the decree of God is for all human beings an applicable remedy, so from this latter those are to be refuted who deny that the death of Christ, and that by the decree of God, is a remedy to be applied to the elect efficaciously and infallibly. For what other sense can there be of these words, He died for the elect efficaciously, than, He died with an absolute intention and efficacious will of saving the elect?
pass_b: A fourth argument is the distinction most received among all theologians: that Christ died for all sufficiently, for the elect efficaciously. Just as from the first half we refuted those who deny that Christ’s death, by God’s decree, is an applicable remedy for all people, so from the second half those must be refuted who deny that Christ’s death, and that by God’s decree, is a remedy to be applied to the elect efficaciously and infallibly. What else can “He died for the elect efficaciously” mean than that he died with an absolute intention and efficacious will to save the elect?
notes_covered: Quartum open; sufficienter/efficaciter distinction; absolute intention for elect

title: Cap. 7 Quartum: not contingent human will—Suarez on intended efficacy
latin: Nam si quis eo torqueat hanc distinctionem, quasi sensus esset, Mortem Christi, quae sufficiens est pro omnibus, in eventu efficacem fieri aliquibus ex contingente actu arbitrii humani; Primo, ipsis verbis refellitur: siquidem, quando dicitur, Christus mortuus est efficaciter pro his aut illis, denotamus singularem efficaciam ex voluntate speciali morientis profluentem, non ex contingente actu credentis dimanantem. Secundo, ab ipsis Jesuitis haec efficacia (ut ita loquar) eventualis non intelligitur in hac distinctione, sed efficacia ab ipso moriente specialiter intenta & promerita. Sic Suarez, In 3. disp. 41. pag. 629. Christus non meruit omnibus remissionem peccatorum quoad efficaciam, quia non applicavit suum meritum, ut omnes infallibiliter talem effectum consequerentur. Mereri igitur efficaciter vel quoad efficaciam est, ea intentione suum meritum applicare aliquibus personis, ut infallibiliter inde effectum vitae aeternae consequantur. Paulo planius, pag. 635. Meritums Christi aequaliter se habet ad omnes quoad sufficientiam, non quoad efficaciam. Quod intelligendum est non tantum in effectibus, qui in uno sit & non in alio, sed etiam ex parte voluntatis, qua Christus ipse diverso modo obtulit sua merita pro diversis. Denique illa omnia testimonia Scripturarum, quae mortem Christi nobis proponunt complicatam cum certo proposito redimendi suas oves, Filios Dei congregandi, Ecclesiam acquirendi, populum peculiarem mundandi & servandi, atque id genus alia a nobis supra commemorata, aperte demonstrant hanc efficaciam de qua loquuntur Theologi, a voluntate morientis Christi esse arcessendam, non ex contingente actu arbitrii humani petendam. Christus speciali quadam intentione oblationis suae impetravit ut electis efficax redderetur; non autem electi in aliqua apprehensione ex libero arbitrio evagante eam sibi reddiderunt efficacem.
pass_a_gloss: For if anyone twists this distinction that way, as if the sense were that the death of Christ, which is sufficient for all, becomes efficacious in the event for some from a contingent act of human free choice; First, it is refuted by the words themselves: seeing that, when it is said, Christ died efficaciously for these or those, we denote a singular efficacy flowing from the special will of the one dying, not issuing from a contingent act of the believer. Secondly, by the Jesuits themselves this (so to speak) eventual efficacy is not understood in this distinction, but efficacy specially intended and merited by the dying one himself. So Suarez, On 3, disp. 41, p. 629: Christ did not merit for all the remission of sins as to efficacy, because he did not apply his merit so that all would infallibly obtain such an effect. To merit therefore efficaciously or as to efficacy is, with that intention, to apply his merit to certain persons so that they may infallibly obtain therefrom the effect of eternal life. A little more plainly, p. 635: The merit of Christ stands equally toward all as to sufficiency, not as to efficacy. Which is to be understood not only in the effects, which are in one and not in another, but also on the part of the will, by which Christ himself offered his merits in a diverse mode for diverse persons. Finally all those testimonies of the Scriptures which set before us the death of Christ joined with a certain purpose of redeeming his sheep, of gathering the sons of God, of acquiring the Church, of cleansing and saving a peculiar people, and things of that kind commemorated by us above, openly demonstrate that this efficacy of which the Theologians speak is to be fetched from the will of the dying Christ, not sought from a contingent act of human free choice. Christ by a certain special intention of his offering obtained that it would be rendered efficacious for the elect; but the elect did not in some apprehension wandering from free choice render it efficacious for themselves.
pass_b: If someone twists the distinction as if Christ’s death, sufficient for all, became efficacious for some only by a contingent act of human free choice, the words themselves refute him: “Christ died efficaciously for these or those” marks a singular efficacy flowing from the dying one’s special will, not from the believer’s contingent act. Second, even the Jesuits do not take “efficacy” in this distinction as mere eventual efficacy, but as efficacy specially intended and merited by the dying one himself. So Suarez (On 3, disp. 41, p. 629): Christ did not merit remission of sins for all as to efficacy, because he did not apply his merit so that all would infallibly gain that effect. To merit efficaciously is to apply his merit to certain persons with the intention that they infallibly obtain eternal life from it. More plainly (p. 635): Christ’s merit stands equally toward all as to sufficiency, not as to efficacy—understood not only in the effects (in one, not another) but also in the will by which Christ offered his merits differently for different persons. Scripture’s witnesses that join Christ’s death to a sure purpose of redeeming his sheep, gathering God’s sons, acquiring the Church, and cleansing a peculiar people show that the efficacy theologians speak of is drawn from the dying Christ’s will, not from contingent free choice. By a special intention in his offering Christ obtained that it be made efficacious for the elect; the elect did not make it efficacious for themselves by some free-choice apprehension.
notes_covered: Anti-contingent-arbitrium twist; Suarez disp. 41; sufficiency vs efficacy; sheep/Church purpose

title: Cap. 7 Quartum Rat. 5: predestination requires special saving regard—Scotus / Malderus
latin: Rat. 5. A Praedestinatione Divina quintam nostram rationem sumemus: Posita siquidem praedestinatione certarum personarum ante jacta mundi fundamenta, necesse est ponere in voluntate Christi seipsum offerentis specialem quendam intuitum & respectum ad salutem eorundem merito suae passionis efficaciter producendam. Nam sive praeponamus electionem Divinam (secundum nostrum intelligendi modum) ipsius passionis decreto, sive postponamus, semper tamen illud firmum manebit, in voluntate Christi, sive passuri, sive patientis, de hisce, sive electis, sive eligendis, efficaciter salvandis fuisse efficacem quandam & singularem intentionem. Christi siquidem voluntas nunquam non conformat se Paternae voluntati. Incredibile ergo est (ut recte Suarez annotavit, In 3. disp. 41. §. 2. pag. 615.) eum aliter obtulisse Christum merita sua pro illis, quos sciebat a Patre electos, quam pro aliis, cum videret voluntatem Patris ut illi infallibiliter salvarentur, & non alii: cui voluntati ipse se in omnibus conformavit. Huc spectant verba Prophetae a nobis modo allata, Esai. liii. 10. Voluntas Domini in manu ejus dirigetur. Electio ergo quorundam ad vitam aeternam, quae est ex gratuita voluntate Dei, habet executionem suam per merita Christi: atque idcirco non est dubitandum, meritoriam Christi mortem fuisse ab ipso Redemtore hisce electis infallibiliter redimendis & servandis specialiter & efficaciter destinatam, atque Patri oblatam. Praeclarum est illud Scoti in hanc sententiam, Lib. 3. dist. 19. pag. 74. Christus praevidit passionem suam Patri offerendam pro praedestinatis & electis, & sic eam efficaciter obtulit in effectu, totaque Trinitas pro eis sic eam efficaciter acceptavit, & pro nullis aliis fuit efficaciter oblata, aut ab aeterno acceptata. Per efficacem oblationem & acceptationem nihil aliud intelligit quam oblationem & acceptationem conjunctam cum absoluto proposito servandi illos pro quibus hunc in modum oblata fuit & acceptata. Malderus Episcopus Antuerpiensis hoc argumento nixus rejicit contrariam illorum sententiam, qui opinantur Christum quoad efficaciam aeque esse mortuum pro omnibus, ac concludit, Supposita praedestinatione illud sequi, Christum hisce praedestinatis longe plus sua morte quam aliis contulisse, pag. 137.
pass_a_gloss: Rat. 5. From Divine Predestination we will take our fifth reason: Seeing that predestination of certain persons before the foundations of the world were laid is posited, it is necessary to posit in the will of Christ offering himself a certain special regard and respect toward producing their salvation efficaciously by the merit of his passion. For whether we place divine election (according to our mode of understanding) before the decree of his passion, or after it, that will always remain firm: that in the will of Christ, whether about to suffer or suffering, concerning these, whether elect or to-be-elected, to be saved efficaciously, there was a certain efficacious and singular intention. For Christ’s will never fails to conform itself to the Father’s will. It is therefore incredible (as Suarez rightly noted, On 3, disp. 41, §2, p. 615) that Christ offered his merits otherwise for those whom he knew elect of the Father than for others, when he saw the Father’s will that they be saved infallibly, and not others: to which will he conformed himself in all things. Hither look the Prophet’s words just cited by us, Isa. 53:10: The will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand. Election of certain ones to eternal life, which is from God’s gracious will, therefore has its execution through Christ’s merits: and therefore it is not to be doubted that Christ’s meritorious death was by the Redeemer himself specially and efficaciously destined for these elect to be infallibly redeemed and saved, and offered to the Father. Excellent is that of Scotus on this sentence, Book 3, dist. 19, p. 74: Christ foresaw his passion to be offered to the Father for the predestinate and elect, and so offered it efficaciously in effect, and the whole Trinity so accepted it efficaciously for them, and for no others was it efficaciously offered, or accepted from eternity. By efficacious offering and acceptance he understands nothing other than offering and acceptance joined with an absolute purpose of saving those for whom it was offered and accepted in this mode. Malderus, Bishop of Antwerp, relying on this argument, rejects the contrary opinion of those who think Christ as to efficacy died equally for all, and concludes that, predestination being supposed, it follows that Christ by his death conferred far more on these predestinate than on others, p. 137.
pass_b: Ratio 5. From divine predestination we take a fifth reason. Given the predestination of certain persons before the world’s foundations, Christ’s will in offering himself must include a special regard for producing their salvation efficaciously by the merit of his passion. Whether we place election before or after the decree of the passion (as we understand the order), this stands: in Christ’s will—whether about to suffer or already suffering—there was an efficacious, singular intention to save these elect (or to-be-elect) efficaciously. His will never fails to conform to the Father’s. So it is incredible (as Suarez notes, On 3, disp. 41, §2, p. 615) that he offered his merits one way for those he knew the Father had chosen and another way for the rest, when he saw the Father’s will that they—and not others—be saved infallibly, and conformed himself to that will in all things. Isaiah 53:10 points here: “The will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand.” Election to eternal life from God’s free will is executed through Christ’s merits; therefore the Redeemer specially and efficaciously destined his meritorious death for these elect to be redeemed and saved infallibly, and offered it to the Father. Scotus puts it well (Book 3, dist. 19, p. 74): Christ foresaw his passion offered to the Father for the predestinate and elect, and so offered it efficaciously in effect; the whole Trinity accepted it efficaciously for them, and for no others was it efficaciously offered or accepted from eternity. By efficacious offering and acceptance he means offering joined to an absolute purpose to save those for whom it was so offered and accepted. Malderus, Bishop of Antwerp, on this argument rejects those who think Christ died equally for all as to efficacy, and concludes (p. 137) that, given predestination, Christ by his death conferred far more on these predestinate than on others.
notes_covered: Rat. 5 praedestinatio; Suarez; Isa 53:10; Scotus dist. 19; Malderus Antwerp

title: Cap. 7 Quartum Rat. 6: offering matches intercession—John 17 / Suarez / Vázquez
latin: Rat. 6. Sexto, argumentari possumus ab illa proportione quae est retinenda inter oblationem Christi pro hominibus, & orationem sive intercessionem pro eisdem. Orasse Christum sive intercessisse apud Patrem suum pro electis, ut fidem firmam & invictam usque ad extremum retinerent, & salutem efficaciter obtinerent, ex Ioann. xvii. atque ex oratione nominatim pro Petro facta, ne fides ejus deficeret, promptum est colligere. Et sane qui eximium illud donum perseverantiae specialibus personis speciali oratione Christi impetratum negaverit, is beneficium omnium beneficiorum spiritualium longe maximum libero arbitrio acceptum referret. Jam hoc posito, illud addam, Sicuti Christus specialiter oravit pro specialibus beneficiis in electos conferendis, ita specialiter seipsum obtulit pro eisdem beneficiis promerendis. De hac oratione & oblatione speciali Suarez ait, In 3. disp. 41. p. 635. Sicut Christus diversimode pro hominibus oravit, ita diversimode meruit: propter quod, licet omnium sit universalis Redemptor, & sufficiens causa salutis, speciali tamen modo est causa efficax salutis eorum quos sibi facit obedientes. Oratio igitur, qua Christus specialiter & efficaciter oravit pro electis, fundamentum habuit in oblatione, qua pro eisdem specialiter & efficaciter sese obtulit. Videtis vim argumenti; Quicquid Christus impetrat singularibus personis per specialem intercessionem, id promeruit iisdem apud Patrem per oblationem suiipsius ad eos specialiter pertinentem: Sed per intercessionem impetrat electis fidem, perseverantiam, ipsam denique salutem: Ergo, ut haec bona illis infallibiliter procuraret, specialiter sese pro iis obtulit. Non dubitat, inquit Vasquez, Christum peculiari oratione & voluntate merita sua illis applicasse qui praedestinati & electi fuerunt, In 1. qu. 23. art. 5. disp. 94. cap. 3.
pass_a_gloss: Rat. 6. Sixth, we can argue from that proportion which is to be kept between Christ’s offering for human beings and his prayer or intercession for the same. That Christ prayed or interceded with his Father for the elect, that they might retain a firm and unconquered faith to the end, and obtain salvation efficaciously, is ready to gather from John 17 and from the prayer made by name for Peter, that his faith might not fail. And truly whoever denies that that excellent gift of perseverance was obtained for special persons by Christ’s special prayer would refer the far greatest of all spiritual benefits to free choice. Now this being posited, I will add this: Just as Christ specially prayed for special benefits to be conferred on the elect, so he specially offered himself for meriting the same benefits. Of this special prayer and offering Suarez says, On 3, disp. 41, p. 635: Just as Christ prayed in diverse modes for human beings, so he merited in diverse modes: on which account, although he is universal Redeemer of all, and a sufficient cause of salvation, yet in a special mode he is the efficacious cause of the salvation of those whom he makes obedient to himself. The prayer, therefore, by which Christ specially and efficaciously prayed for the elect, had its foundation in the offering by which for the same he specially and efficaciously offered himself. You see the force of the argument; Whatever Christ obtains for singular persons by special intercession, that he merited for the same with the Father by an offering of himself specially pertaining to them: But by intercession he obtains for the elect faith, perseverance, and finally salvation itself: Therefore, that he might infallibly procure these goods for them, he specially offered himself for them. Vázquez does not doubt, he says, that Christ by peculiar prayer and will applied his merits to those who were predestinate and elect, On 1, q. 23, art. 5, disp. 94, ch. 3.
pass_b: Ratio 6. Sixth, keep the proportion between Christ’s offering for people and his prayer or intercession for them. From John 17, and from his named prayer for Peter that Peter’s faith not fail, it is plain that Christ interceded with the Father for the elect to keep a firm, unconquered faith to the end and obtain salvation efficaciously. Anyone who denies that the gift of perseverance was won for special persons by Christ’s special prayer would credit free choice with the greatest of all spiritual benefits. That granted, I add: just as Christ specially prayed for special benefits for the elect, so he specially offered himself to merit those same benefits. On this special prayer and offering Suarez says (On 3, disp. 41, p. 635): as Christ prayed in different ways for people, so he merited in different ways; though he is universal Redeemer of all and a sufficient cause of salvation, in a special mode he is the efficacious cause of salvation for those he makes obedient. So the prayer by which he specially and efficaciously prayed for the elect rests on the offering by which he specially and efficaciously offered himself for them. See the force: whatever Christ obtains for particular persons by special intercession, he merited for them with the Father by an offering specially pertaining to them. By intercession he obtains for the elect faith, perseverance, and salvation itself; therefore, to procure those goods for them infallibly, he specially offered himself for them. Vázquez does not doubt (On 1, q. 23, art. 5, disp. 94, ch. 3) that by peculiar prayer and will Christ applied his merits to those who were predestinate and elect.

title: Cap. 7 Quartum Rat. 7: death as medium tracks God’s diverse saving will
latin: Rat. 7. Christi mors meritumque est medium a Deo ordinatum ad exequendum & implendum aeternum Dei consilium de salute hominum. Si igitur Dei voluntas diversimode se habeat ad salutem hominum efficiendam, tum & mors Christi ab eodem diversimode intendetur in salutem humanam, diversimode applicabitur. Media siquidem semper adhibentur in ordine ad finem: & juxta intentionem agentis erit modus applicationis. Jam certum est & in confesso apud omnes sanos Theologos, Deum non eo modo velle salutem omnium quo vult salutem aliquorum: Ergo neque medium quo salutem humanam procurandam decrevit, scilicet mortem Christi, ita omnibus applicatum voluit sicut aliquibus. Unde liquet iis quibus Deus efficaci voluntate salutem decrevit, Christi mortem fuisse ita destinatam, ut merito ejusdem omnia ad salutem infallibiliter producendam necessaria ex eadem ad eos redundarent: Et e contra, quibus tali voluntate salutem minime decrevit, iis neque mortem Christi fuisse ad eundem modum destinatam. Mors igitur Christi ex speciali intentione Dei Patris illud sacrificium ad salutem hominum ordinantis, & Christi seipsum offerentis, ac Paternae voluntati conformantis, aliter electis destinata & applicata intelligitur, quos Deus decrevit per hanc mortem infallibiliter servare, aliter ceteris, quos Deus non impedit quin hac morte permittit suo vitio perire. Quisquis negat mortem Christi hoc discrimine oblatam pro hominibus, & applicatam ipsis hominibus, ille eadem opera negare potest Deum sapientissimum & potentissimum aut nosse aut posse media a se instituta, prout diversa ratio voluntatis suae exigit, diversimode diversis hominibus intendere & accommodare.
pass_a_gloss: Rat. 7. The death and merit of Christ is a medium ordained by God for executing and fulfilling God’s eternal counsel concerning the salvation of human beings. If therefore God’s will stands diversely toward effecting the salvation of human beings, then also the death of Christ will by the same be intended diversely toward human salvation, and applied diversely. For media are always employed in order to the end: and according to the intention of the agent will be the mode of application. Now it is certain and confessed among all sound Theologians that God does not will the salvation of all in that mode in which he wills the salvation of some: Therefore neither did he will the medium by which he decreed human salvation to be procured, namely the death of Christ, applied to all just as to some. Whence it is clear that for those for whom God by efficacious will decreed salvation, the death of Christ was so destined that by its merit all things necessary for producing salvation infallibly would redound from it to them: And on the contrary, for those for whom by such will he by no means decreed salvation, for them neither was the death of Christ destined in the same mode. The death of Christ therefore, from the special intention of God the Father ordaining that sacrifice to the salvation of human beings, and of Christ offering himself and conforming to the Father’s will, is understood destined and applied otherwise to the elect, whom God decreed to save infallibly through this death, otherwise to the rest, whom God does not prevent from perishing by their own fault even with this death. Whoever denies that the death of Christ was offered for human beings and applied to human beings themselves with this discrimination, by the same stroke can deny that God most wise and most powerful either knows or can intend and accommodate media instituted by himself to diverse human beings diversely, as the diverse reason of his will requires.
pass_b: Ratio 7. Christ’s death and merit is the means God ordained to carry out his eternal counsel for human salvation. If God’s will stands differently toward effecting people’s salvation, then Christ’s death is likewise intended and applied differently toward that end. Means always serve the end, and the mode of application follows the agent’s intention. All sound theologians confess that God does not will everyone’s salvation in the same mode in which he wills some people’s. Therefore he did not will the means—Christ’s death—applied to all as it is applied to some. So for those for whom God by efficacious will decreed salvation, Christ’s death was destined so that by its merit everything needed to produce salvation infallibly would flow to them; for those for whom he did not so decree salvation, Christ’s death was not destined in that same mode. From the Father’s special intention in ordaining that sacrifice, and from Christ’s self-offering conformed to the Father’s will, the death is understood as destined and applied one way to the elect, whom God decreed to save infallibly through it, and another way to the rest, whom he allows to perish by their own fault even with this death. Whoever denies that discrimination in the offering and application can as easily deny that the wisest and most powerful God knows how—or is able—to intend and fit the means he instituted to different people as his will’s different reason requires.

title: Cap. 7 Quartum Rat. 8: fruitful application proves antecedent intention—Phil 2:13 / John 15:5
latin: Rat. 8. Certum est ex eventu, quosdam homines mortem Christi cum infinito ejusdem merito realiter & efficaciter ad salutem sibi applicare. Quaero igitur utrum haec applicatio facta sit secundum antecedaneam & efficacem intentionem Christi in cruce seipsum offerentis, an contra eandem, sive absque eadem praecedente. Si concesserint in Christo moriente antecedaneam & specialem voluntatem de hac efficaci applicatione quae omnibus electis, & solis electis contingit, habemus id ipsum quod evincere conamur, nempe hanc mortem ex speciali intentione Dei & Christi electis ut efficaciter applicandam destinari. Jam vero, contra Christi intentionem posse ullum hominem mortem ejus sibi efficaciter applicare, nemo dixerit. Id unum reliquum est, ut dicant fieri hanc applicationem efficacem ab iisdem hominibus pro libertate suae voluntatis absque praecedente ulla speciali & efficaci intentione Divinae voluntatis. At pietas vetat hoc asserere: Primo, quia in actibus bonis & salutiferis efficax Dei voluntas se habet antecedenter ad efficacem voluntatem humanam. Deus enim est qui in nobis operatur & velle & perficere, Phil. ii. 13. nec quicquam operatur in nobis antecedenter, quod non antecedenter decrevit operari. Secundo, quia in operibus hisce ad salutem pertinentibus nihil possumus sine Christo: Ioann. xv. 5. Sine me nihil potestis facere. At quod possumus per Christum, ejus rei faciundae potestatem accipimus propter Christi meritum: quod absque antecedanea & speciali intentione Christi morientis & merentis nemini assignatur. Quicunque igitur eximiam hanc gratiam obtinuit, meritum Christi sibi jam efficaciter applicaverit, fateri debet, se hanc ipsam applicandi facultatem prae aliis accepisse a speciali benignitate Dei Christique hoc suum meritum specialiter illi intendentis, destinantis, applicantis. Sic ipse eventus fructuosae applicationis in praedestinatis demonstrat fuisse in Christo offerente seipsum, & Deo acceptante hoc sacrificium, specialem & efficacem intentionem ejusdem applicationis quoad praedestinatos. Atque hoc est illud ipsum singulare privilegium electorum in morte Christi quod hac thesi nostra conamur stabilire.
pass_a_gloss: Rat. 8. It is certain from the event that certain human beings really and efficaciously apply to themselves for salvation the death of Christ with its infinite merit. I ask therefore whether this application was made according to the antecedent and efficacious intention of Christ offering himself on the cross, or against the same, or without the same preceding. If they concede in the dying Christ an antecedent and special will concerning this efficacious application which befalls all the elect and the elect alone, we have that very thing we are trying to prove, namely that this death by the special intention of God and Christ is destined to the elect as to be applied efficaciously. But now, that any human being can efficaciously apply his death to himself against Christ’s intention, no one will say. This alone remains, that they say this efficacious application is made by those same human beings according to the liberty of their will without any preceding special and efficacious intention of the Divine will. But piety forbids asserting this: First, because in good and saving acts God’s efficacious will stands antecedently to the efficacious human will. For it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish, Phil. 2:13. nor does he work anything in us antecedently which he did not antecedently decree to work. Secondly, because in these works pertaining to salvation we can do nothing without Christ: John 15:5. Without me you can do nothing. But what we can do through Christ, we receive the power of doing that thing on account of Christ’s merit: which without the antecedent and special intention of Christ dying and meriting is assigned to no one. Whoever therefore has obtained this excellent grace, and has already efficaciously applied Christ’s merit to himself, ought to confess that he received this very faculty of applying before others from the special kindness of God and of Christ specially intending, destining, and applying this his merit to him. Thus the very event of fruitful application in the predestinate demonstrates that there was in Christ offering himself, and in God accepting this sacrifice, a special and efficacious intention of the same application as to the predestinate. And this is that very singular privilege of the elect in the death of Christ which by this our thesis we are trying to establish.
pass_b: Ratio 8. The event shows that some people really and efficaciously apply Christ’s death, with its infinite merit, to themselves for salvation. Was that application made according to Christ’s antecedent, efficacious intention in offering himself on the cross—or against it, or without it preceding? If they grant in the dying Christ an antecedent special will for this efficacious application that falls to all the elect and to them alone, we have what we aim to prove: that by God’s and Christ’s special intention this death is destined for the elect as to be applied efficaciously. No one will say a person can apply Christ’s death to himself efficaciously against Christ’s intention. The only remaining claim is that people make the application efficacious by free will without any preceding special, efficacious intention of the divine will. Piety forbids that. First, in good and saving acts God’s efficacious will stands before the human: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish” (Phil. 2:13), and he works nothing in us antecedently that he did not antecedently decree to work. Second, in works that belong to salvation we can do nothing without Christ: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). What we can do through Christ we receive power to do because of Christ’s merit—which, without the dying and meriting Christ’s antecedent special intention, is assigned to no one. So whoever has obtained this excellent grace and already applied Christ’s merit to himself efficaciously must confess he received that applying faculty above others from the special kindness of God and of Christ, who specially intended, destined, and applied his merit to him. The fruitful application in the predestinate itself shows that in Christ offering himself, and in God accepting the sacrifice, there was a special efficacious intention of that application for the predestinate. And that is the singular privilege of the elect in Christ’s death this thesis aims to establish.
notes_covered: Rat. 8 event application; Phil 2:13; John 15:5; antecedent intention; elect privilege

title: Cap. 7 Quartum Rat. 9: without merited application elect have no privilege—Bannes / Rom 8:32
latin: Rat. 9. Si ponamus Christi mortem ex ordinatione Dei & intentione Christi non meruisse praedestinatis efficacem applicationem, & infallibilem salutis consecutionem inde emanantem, illud incommodi sequetur, hoc meritum Mediatoris, juxta voluntatem & intentionem Patris illud acceptantis Filiiique illud exhibentis, non magis spectare ad electos quam praeteritos, sed ex aequo ad utrosque pertingere. Patet consequentia, quia concessum est, Ex voluntate Dei meritum Christi morientis ad omnes homines se extendere sub hac conditione, Si per fidem illud sibi applicaverint. Nisi ergo Christus morte sua intenderit electis hoc insuper mereri, ut per Fidem donatam fiat in illis haec fructuosa applicatio, nullum singulare privilegium in merito Christi illis assignatur. Nam Christi mors ex ordinatione Dei Iudae hoc meruit, ut potuerit sub conditione Fidei ad vitam aeternam pervenire: Petro igitur & illud insuper obtinuit, ut propter meritum Christi fidem perseverantem acciperet, caeteraque omnia spiritualia beneficia quae ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter consequendam requiruntur. Atque huc spectat illa Apostoli ratiocinatio, Rom. viii. 32. Ubi de praedestinatorum privilegiis disserit, Qui proprio Filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit eum, quomodo non etiam cum eo omnia nobis donabit? Quo in loco sicut specialem quandam vocationem praedestinatorum antea innuuerat, quam appellavit vocationem secundum propositum, ita & specialem quandam oblationem Christi pro eisdem praedestinatis designat, quam licet appellare oblationem secundum propositum, id est, cum proposito certo gratiam efficacem conferendi electis, eosdemque merito hujus mortis ad vitam infallibiliter perducendi. Qui tollunt hoc discrimen intentionis Divinae, quoad mortem Christi, in relatione ad electos & praeteritos consideratam, illi, (ut vere Bannesius In 1. quaest. 23. art. 5. pag. 296. 297.) faciunt meritum Christi nihilo perfectius esse causam salutis praedestinatorum quam reproborum. Quia quod attinet ad sufficientiam meriti, aeque respicit omnes; sed differentia est in hoc, quod quibusdam applicatur illud meritum, quibusdam vero non. Ergo (si applicatio ipsa quoad electos non cadat sub merito Christi) meritum Christi aequaliter respiciet praedestinatos & reprobes. Haec ille.
pass_a_gloss: Rat. 9. If we posit that the death of Christ by God’s ordination and Christ’s intention did not merit for the predestinate an efficacious application and an infallible obtaining of salvation flowing therefrom, this inconvenience will follow: that this merit of the Mediator, according to the will and intention of the Father accepting it and of the Son exhibiting it, does not regard the elect more than the passed-by, but reaches equally to both. The consequence is plain, because it is granted that by God’s will the merit of the dying Christ extends to all human beings under this condition, If by faith they apply it to themselves. Unless therefore Christ by his death intended for the elect to merit this besides, that through faith given this fruitful application be made in them, no singular privilege in Christ’s merit is assigned to them. For Christ’s death by God’s ordination merited this for Judas, that he could under the condition of Faith arrive at eternal life: for Peter therefore it obtained that besides, that on account of Christ’s merit he receive persevering faith, and all the other spiritual benefits required for infallibly obtaining eternal life. And hither looks that reasoning of the Apostle, Rom. 8:32, where he discusses the privileges of the predestinate: He who spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not also with him give us all things? In which place, just as he had earlier hinted a certain special calling of the predestinate, which he called a calling according to purpose, so also he designates a certain special offering of Christ for the same predestinate, which one may call an offering according to purpose, that is, with a certain purpose of conferring efficacious grace on the elect, and of leading the same infallibly to life by the merit of this death. Those who remove this discrimination of Divine intention as to Christ’s death, considered in relation to the elect and the passed-by, those (as Báñez truly, On 1, q. 23, art. 5, pp. 296–297) make the merit of Christ no more perfect a cause of the salvation of the predestinate than of the reprobate. Because as to the sufficiency of the merit, it equally regards all; but the difference is in this, that to some that merit is applied, to others not. Therefore (if the application itself as to the elect does not fall under Christ’s merit) Christ’s merit will equally regard the predestinate and the reprobate. Thus he.
pass_b: Ratio 9. Suppose Christ’s death, by God’s ordination and Christ’s intention, did not merit for the predestinate an efficacious application and the infallible obtaining of salvation that flows from it. Then this follows: the Mediator’s merit, under the Father’s accepting will and the Son’s exhibiting will, regards the elect no more than the passed-by, but reaches both alike. The consequence is clear, since it is granted that by God’s will the dying Christ’s merit extends to all under the condition: if by faith they apply it to themselves. Unless Christ by his death also meant to merit for the elect that, through faith given, this fruitful application be made in them, no singular privilege in his merit is assigned to them. By God’s ordination Christ’s death merited for Judas that he could, under the condition of faith, reach eternal life; for Peter it obtained besides that, because of Christ’s merit, he receive persevering faith and all other spiritual benefits required to obtain eternal life infallibly. Paul’s reasoning in Romans 8:32 looks here, treating the predestinate’s privileges: “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him give us all things?” Just as he had hinted a special calling of the predestinate—“according to purpose”—so he marks a special offering of Christ for those same predestinate, an offering according to purpose: with a sure purpose to confer efficacious grace on the elect and lead them infallibly to life by this death’s merit. Those who erase that discrimination of divine intention in Christ’s death toward elect and passed-by, as Báñez truly says (On 1, q. 23, art. 5, pp. 296–297), make Christ’s merit no more perfect a cause of the predestinate’s salvation than of the reprobate’s. As to sufficiency the merit regards all equally; the difference is that it is applied to some and not to others. So if application itself for the elect does not fall under Christ’s merit, that merit regards predestinate and reprobate alike. So Báñez.
notes_covered: Rat. 9; Judas vs Peter; Rom 8:32 offering according to purpose; Bannes ST I q.23; before Rat. 10
